Aims The potential of mechanistic biomarkers to improve prediction of drug‐induced liver injury (DILI) and hepatic regeneration is widely acknowledged. We sought to determine reference intervals for new biomarkers of DILI and regeneration, as well as to characterize their natural variability and impact of diurnal variation. Methods Serum samples from 227 healthy volunteers were recruited as part of a cross‐sectional study; of these, 25 subjects had weekly serial sampling over 3 weeks, while 23 had intensive blood sampling over a 24h period. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), MicroRNA‐122 (miR‐122), High Mobility Group Box‐1 (HMGB1), total Keratin‐18 (K18), caspase‐cleaved Keratin‐18 (ccK18), Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH) and Macrophage Colony‐Stimulating Factor‐1 (CSF‐1) were assayed. Results Reference intervals were established for each biomarker based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI) following the assessment of fixed effects in univariate and multivariable models. Intra‐individual variability was found to be non‐significant, and there was no significant impact of diurnal variation. Conclusion Reference intervals for novel DILI biomarkers have been described. An upper limit of a reference range might represent the most appropriate mechanism to utilize these data. What is already known about this subject Potential for novel biomarkers to improve prediction of drug‐induced liver injury (DILI) is widely acknowledged. It is necessary that reference intervals for these biomarkers are defined in several healthy human populations. What this study adds Our study reports reference intervals for novel biomarkers of DILI in healthy volunteers. We report a reference interval for biomarker HGMB1 in healthy volunteers. Data will be a useful point of reference when interpreting exploratory clinical DILI studies. Data can also be used when seeking biomarker qualification by regulatory authorities. 1 INTRODUCTION Drug‐induced liver injury (DILI) represents a major cause of patient morbidity and mortality and is a serious concern for patients, clinicians and the pharmaceutical industry. 1 , 2 It accounts for over half of the acute liver failure cases observed in Western countries and is a leading cause of withdrawal postmarketing. 1 , 2 Assessment of liver injury and repair has to date relied on a small number of blood‐based markers. These include serum alanine and aspartate aminotransferase activity (ALT and AST, respectively) as indicators of hepatocellular injury; alkaline phosphatase (ALP), γ‐glutamyl transferase (GGT) and total bilirubin (TBIL) for assessment of cholestatic injury; prothrombin time as a marker of liver synthetic capacity. 3 , 4 However, the lack of sensitivity and specificity of these tests, together with the fact that they provide little information about the mechanistic basis of liver injury, are significant limitations in using them for prediction and understanding DILI. Furthermore, elevation of these markers can be a result of disease/injury in nonhepatic sites, 5 and the markers are of limited prognostic value. A number of new biomarkers have shown promise in exploratory studies and preliminary evaluations, using samples from patients with liver injury during clinical trials and clinical practice. 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 These include biomarkers that provide enhanced hepatic specificity such as microRNA‐122 (miR‐122), 11 biomarkers that can be used to monitor apoptotic‐necrotic dynamics such as keratin‐18 (K18), caspase‐cleaved K18 (ccK18) 9 , 10 and high mobility group box‐1 (HMGB1), mitochondrial dysfunction (glutamate dehydrogenase; GLDH), 8 , 9 and proteins that promote hepatic regeneration such as macrophage colony‐stimulating factor (CSF‐1). Both miR‐122 and GLDH are potential liver‐specific alternatives to ALT, having performed well as biomarkers for hepatocellular injury, particularly in patients with DILI resulting from paracetamol overdose 12 , 13 , 14 . The measurement of apoptotic vs . necrotic cell death using circulating K18 levels has also provided insights into the mechanistic basis of DILI in man. 8 , 15 Recent work has demonstrated the potential utility of these novel biomarkers, with a 3‐biomarker multivariate linear regression model achieving near perfect separation between patients with liver damage following paracetamol overdose and healthy controls (receiver operator characteristic, area under the curve = 0.99). 10 Furthermore, this 3‐biomarker model confirmed strong predictability and specificity when comparing patients with liver damage to patient cohorts with muscle, pancreas, gastrointestinal and kidney damage (receiver operator characteristic, area under the curve = 0.98). 10 Based on these observations, there has been significant interest and investment by biomarker consortia and DILI researcher networks to further develop and qualify novel DILI biomarker candidates that can add value, including mechanistic understanding, to current assessment methods. Importantly, these candidate biomarkers have been underpinned by supportive preclinical science 9 , 16 , 17 and more recently, letters of support from regulatory authorities have backed the continued development and qualification of these candidate biomarkers across the spectrum of DILI observed in man. 13 , 14 Reference intervals in healthy volunteers were first reported by Church et al . as part of a larger investigation into the aforementioned biomarkers as candidate biomarkers for DILI. 9 K18, ccK18 and miR‐122 levels in many healthy volunteers were found to be below the lower limit of quantification. Furthermore, miR‐122 demonstrated high inter‐ and intrasubject variability, which raised questions about its application and interpretation as a candidate biomarker for DILI. Given the potential utility of these biomarkers, it is important that reference intervals are defined in several healthy human populations, to aid further qualification of new biomarkers of liver injury or regeneration, so they can be appropriately interpreted in patients with DILI. As such, the aim of this current investigation was to establish reference intervals for miR122, GLDH, K18, ccK18, HMGB1 and CSF‐1, in a healthy human volunteer cohort and to assess the impact of inter‐ and intraindividual variation, and diurnal variation.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study aimed to establish comprehensive reference intervals for novel circulating biomarkers of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) and hepatic regeneration in healthy human volunteers. It investigated intra- and interindividual variability, as well as diurnal variation, to provide robust data for interpreting exploratory clinical DILI studies and assisting biomarker qualification by regulatory authorities.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Observational study for establishing reference intervals of circulating biomarkers
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved serum sample collection from 227 healthy volunteers in a cross-sectional study (single sample). Additionally, 25 subjects underwent weekly serial sampling over 3 weeks, and 23 subjects had intensive 24-hour blood sampling every 3 hours after a 10-h overnight fast and standardized meals. No therapeutic interventions or dose comparisons were involved, as the focus was on establishing reference intervals and assessing natural variability in healthy subjects.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reference intervals established; consistent with previous values but influenced by sex and BMI; intra-individual variability non-significant; no significant diurnal impact.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference intervals based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI) and consistent with previously described values. Intra-individual variability found to be non-significant, and no significant diurnal variation. A significant impact of sex and BMI on observed ALT values was noted.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Standard clinical chemistry marker for assessing hepatocellular injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Establishing reference ranges in healthy human volunteers to characterize natural variability and diurnal variation, including fixed effects of sex and BMI.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates hepatocellular injury, but is not liver-specific; can be elevated in non-liver diseases. Reference intervals are useful for interpreting exploratory clinical DILI studies, with sex and BMI being significant factors.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reference intervals established; influenced by sex and BMI; lower intraindividual variability compared to previous studies.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference intervals based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI). Sex and BMI were identified as significant fixed effects in multivariable models. Intraindividual variability was 41%, lower than previously reported (94%). No significant impact of diurnal variation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enriched in the liver, acting as a mechanism-based biomarker of hepatocellular injury and regeneration; potential liver-specific alternative to ALT.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Establishing healthy reference intervals in human volunteers, assessing intra- and interindividual variability and diurnal variation, and identifying the effect of sex and BMI on serum levels.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential to improve DILI prediction and hepatic regeneration assessment. Reference intervals should account for sex and BMI for accurate diagnostic interpretation and clinical use.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reference intervals established; levels significantly influenced by age; intra-individual variability non-significant; consistent with previous large studies.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference intervals based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI) and consistent with previous studies. Age was identified as a significant fixed effect contributing to interindividual variability. Intra-individual variability found to be non-significant, with no significant impact of diurnal variation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Monitors apoptotic-necrotic dynamics; associated with DILI and biological processes where age is a factor for variability.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Establishing reference ranges in healthy human volunteers, characterizing natural variability, diurnal variation, and the influence of age on serum levels.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential to improve DILI prediction and hepatic regeneration assessment. Age is a key factor for interindividual variability, suggesting age-stratified reference intervals are necessary for accurate diagnostic interpretation.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reference intervals established; levels not significantly influenced by demographic factors in this study, but high variability across studies observed.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference intervals based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI). No significant fixed effects of sex, age, height, weight, BMI, or ethnicity were observed. Intra-individual variability found to be non-significant. High variability in mean K18 levels across studies, suggesting influence of ubiquitous expression.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Monitors apoptotic-necrotic dynamics, reflecting the degree of hepatocellular necrotic and/or apoptotic injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Establishing reference ranges in healthy human volunteers, characterizing natural variability, diurnal variation, and assessing its stability across demographic factors.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Identifies hepatocellular necrotic and/or apoptotic injury. Ubiquitous expression may contribute to high variability, but stable levels across demographics in this study support universal reference intervals for DILI prediction and hepatic regeneration assessment.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reference intervals established; consistent levels observed, not significantly influenced by demographic factors; intra-individual variability non-significant.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference intervals based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI). No significant fixed effects of sex, age, height, weight, BMI, or ethnicity were observed. Mean ccK18 levels were consistent with previous studies. Intra-individual variability found to be non-significant, with no significant impact of diurnal variation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Monitors apoptotic-necrotic dynamics, reflecting the degree of hepatocellular necrotic and/or apoptotic injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Establishing reference ranges in healthy human volunteers, characterizing natural variability, diurnal variation, and assessing its stability across demographic factors.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Identifies hepatocellular necrotic and/or apoptotic injury. Stable levels across various demographic factors and low intraindividual variability support the establishment of universal reference intervals for DILI prediction and hepatic regeneration assessment.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reference intervals established; levels significantly influenced by BMI; lower intra- and interindividual variability compared to previous reports; no significant diurnal impact.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference intervals based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI). BMI was identified as a significant fixed effect from linear modelling. Intra-individual variability found to be non-significant, and no significant diurnal variation. No significant intra- or interindividual variation across the study, in contrast to previously reported problems.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Enriched in the liver, acting as a mechanism-based biomarker of liver injury and regeneration; indicator of mitochondrial dysfunction; potential liver-specific alternative to ALT.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Establishing healthy reference intervals in human volunteers, assessing intra- and interindividual variability and diurnal variation, and identifying the effect of BMI on serum levels.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential to improve DILI prediction and hepatic regeneration assessment. Reference intervals should account for BMI to reduce variability and improve interpretation, especially due to visceral fat influencing liver function.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Reference intervals established; levels not significantly influenced by demographic factors; intra-individual variability non-significant; higher mean level than previously reported, potentially due to sample collection methods.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Reference intervals based on the 97.5% quantile (90% CI). No significant fixed effects of sex, age, height, weight, BMI, or ethnicity were observed. Intra-individual variability found to be non-significant, with no significant impact of diurnal variation. Mean serum level was 12.18 ng/mL, significantly higher than previously reported (0.251 ng/mL), suggesting potential loss during clotting.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Promotes hepatic regeneration; diagnostic marker for certain cancers.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Establishing reference ranges in healthy human volunteers, characterizing natural variability, diurnal variation, and assessing its stability across demographic factors, also noting potential issues with sample collection.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential to improve DILI prediction and hepatic regeneration assessment. Supports universal reference intervals due to stable levels across demographics. Also a sensitive diagnostic marker for pancreatic and ampullary cancer. Awareness of potential loss during serum clotting is crucial for accurate measurement.
